items.title: In Connect Sync and Cloud Sync coexistence, the Cloud Sync agent handles every password writeback
items.officialTitle: When Microsoft Entra Connect Cloud Sync and Microsoft Entra Connect Sync coexist and are configured for the same domain, all password writeback operations for users synchronized from that domain are processed by the Cloud Sync agent.

items.tier0Note: In a coexistence deployment the Cloud Sync agent, not the Connect Sync server, is the process that writes password resets into AD DS for that domain. The tier-0 write path moves to the Cloud Sync agent host, and any hardening, monitoring or break-glass procedure still aimed only at the Connect Sync server now watches the wrong machine.
items.fingerprint: On 7 September 2026 Microsoft added a NOTE to concept-sspr-writeback stating that where Cloud Sync and Connect Sync coexist for the same domain, all password writeback for that domain is processed by the Cloud Sync agent.

items.fingerprint: The September 2026 security update is available for all supported Windows versions. The update expands high confidence device targeting data for new Secure Boot certificates and improves the servicing stack; a limited number of devices may take one additional restart after the Secure Boot certificate update is applied.

graphMap.rule: resource = first path segment that is not a parameter; /me/... counts as users. Directory action microsoft.directory/<resource>[/<property>]/<operation>; a .unified or .security suffix on the resource falls back to its base. GET maps to read, POST to create, PATCH and PUT to update, DELETE to delete. A role covers an endpoint when it holds an action on the same resource with the same operation, or allTasks on that resource. Coverage is the share of the permission's ENDPOINTS, never the count of the role's actions. Depth is whole resource when the matching action carries allProperties or allTasks, and selected properties only otherwise.
graphMap.ruleNote: Derived by this brief, not published by Microsoft. Microsoft publishes no role-to-permission mapping: permissions.json carries authorizationType, ownerInfo, pathSets and schemes and no role field at all, and the 136 role source files in MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs name no Graph permission.

components.name: Entra Connect Sync
components.deadlineNote: All synchronization services in Microsoft Entra Connect Sync stop working on 30 September 2026 on any server below 2.5.79.0. A server on 2.6.84.0 does not breach the requirement.

items.text: Added support for phishing-resistant authentication methods in the Microsoft Entra Connect setup wizard (preview). Administrators can now sign in using passkeys and FIDO2 security keys through Windows Web Account Manager (WAM) when configuring Microsoft Entra Connect.
Added support for the France sovereign cloud environment, including Pass-through Authentication, Seamless Single Sign-On, password writeback, and Health Agent monitoring.

Improved the auto-upgrade process to preserve customer modifications to configuration files. Previously, auto-upgrade overwrote the miiserver.exe.config file, discarding any manual customizations. The system now merges customer modifications with the new configuration and validates the result before applying.

Improved the setup process for Application-Based Authentication to handle Trusted Platform Module (TPM)-backed certificates. The system now tests a certificate's signing capability upfront and handles TPM signature verification correctly.

Microsoft Entra Connect setup wizard no longer silently falls back to the legacy directory synchronization account when Application-Based Authentication setup fails. The wizard now stops with an error so the underlying issue can be resolved.

Microsoft Entra Connect no longer automatically switches existing servers from the legacy directory synchronization account to Application-Based Authentication during background sync. New installations continue to configure Application-Based Authentication during setup.

PowerShell cmdlets that modify cloud configuration (Set-ADSyncAADCompanyFeature, Set-ADSyncAADPasswordSyncState) now require explicit -AADUsername for interactive admin authentication. The setup wizard uses interactive Microsoft Authentication Library (MSAL) authentication for cloud writes instead of stored service credentials.

Removed Password Hash Synchronization (PHS) self-healing. PHS no longer automatically re-enables its cloud feature flag in the background. If the PHS cloud feature flag is disabled, an administrator must explicitly re-enable it.
Updated the bundled MSAL from version 4.64.1 to 4.83.3.
Upgraded the bundled SQL LocalDB from SQL Server 2019 to SQL Server 2022.
Upgraded the Visual C++ redistributable from version 12 (2013) to version 14.42.34438 (2015-2022).
Removed the Visual C++ 2013 redistributable dependency.
Fixed an issue in the PowerShell diagnostic HTML report rendering.
Fixed an issue in the Synchronization Service Manager metaverse search.
Improved Application-Based Authentication setup on servers with non-conforming TPM firmware by falling back to a software-based certificate when the TPM cannot produce a valid signature.
Fixed an issue where Generic SQL (GSQL) connector profile creation failed because required profile parameters were not populated during configuration.

Fixed an issue where the Application Proxy cloud name was not correctly resolved in the France cloud environment, causing Pass-through Authentication registration to fail with an EnvironmentName attribute is invalid error.
Fixed an issue where the China cloud instance name was not correctly resolved by the Discovery Endpoint API, which could cause cloud instance detection to fail.
Fixed an issue where admin actions audit logging captured the service account identity instead of the actual administrator performing the action for Synchronization Rule changes.
Fixed multiple security vulnerabilities in bundled third-party dependencies.

Fixed a known issue where auto-upgrade could stop your Microsoft Entra Connect server unexpectedly. Auto-upgrade now detects modifications to the miiserver.exe.config and miisclient.exe.config configuration files and skips automatic upgrade on those servers.

catalog.note: Morning pass, Wednesday 9 September 2026 at 06:35 Warsaw, compared against the afternoon pass of 8 September at 21:20. All four upstream sources were re-cloned and re-parsed in code this morning and all four are unchanged. MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs moved from HEAD ef8e760 to ef9e28e, but nothing under docs/identity/role-based-access-control moved with it: 140 second-level headings, 136 roles, 133 Actions tables, 1,963 actions, 147 privileged action rows, 34 privileged role headers and 5 Where this role applies tables, every figure recounted and identical. microsoftgraph/microsoft-graph-docs-contrib is still at 4ad99fd: 939 permission sections plus 58 resource-specific-consent rows, 997 documented names. microsoftgraph/microsoft-graph-devx-content is still at 0c140cd: 925 permissions, 1,507 schemes, 24,117 method-and-path pairs over 7,440 paths. merill/microsoft-info is still at 6b40492 of 7 September 20:42 UTC: 731 application roles, 815 delegated scopes, 972 in union. So Microsoft changed nothing in either catalog today, and the three change arrays are empty on purpose. One correction the run made to its own arithmetic and not to Microsoft's: a first parse read 35 privileged role headers because it matched the privileged label wherever it appeared in a role's file, including inside an action row. Only the label above the autogenerated table marks the role itself, which restores 34. That was a parser fault here; the Authentication Extensibility Password Administrator role header still carries no privileged label. The only movement in the catalog today is one queued API surface, Azure Storage, inventoried here for the first time.

comparedWith.label: afternoon pass of 8 September 2026 at 21:20 Warsaw
comparedWith.method: Both catalogs were rebuilt from Microsoft's own files, not from the previous page: the role reference and its 139 include files from a sparse blobless clone of MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs, the Graph permission reference from microsoftgraph/microsoft-graph-docs-contrib, the permission-to-endpoint map from microsoftgraph/microsoft-graph-devx-content, and the live service surface from the merill/microsoft-info dump. Each parse was diffed by name set against the carried catalog.
comparedWith.note: Every entry below was carried forward from the page named here. Where a value is unchanged the entry was copied byte for byte and neither its version nor its lastChanged was touched, which is why both catalog versions stand still today. A quiet catalog is a result, not an omission.

roles.note: Microsoft's own role source files were re-cloned from MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on 9 September 2026 (repository HEAD ef9e28e) and parsed by script from permissions-reference.md and the 139 per-role include files, not by eye. The reference carries 140 second-level headings; four of them — All roles, Deprecated roles, Roles not shown in the portal and Next steps — are page sections rather than roles, leaving 136 built-in Entra directory roles. 133 have an Actions table and 3 do not, those 3 being the Purview Workload Content Administrator, Reader and Writer roles. 1,963 documented directory actions, 147 action rows carrying Microsoft's privileged label, 34 roles carrying that label in their own header, 5 roles with a Where this role applies table. Every one of those figures was recounted in code today and is identical to yesterday's parse. The repository HEAD moved from ef8e760 to ef9e28e overnight, but nothing under the role directory moved with it. complete is false because the inventory also carries one role that Microsoft's reference does not list.

graph.note: Sixteen API surfaces, one of them — Azure Storage — read for the first time today. Microsoft Graph's documented set was re-parsed in code from Microsoft's own source file (microsoftgraph/microsoft-graph-docs-contrib, concepts/permissions-reference.md, repository HEAD 4ad99fd) on 9 September 2026: 939 permission sections plus the 58-row resource-specific-consent table, 997 documented names, the two sets disjoint, identical name for name to yesterday. The service side did not move either: merill/microsoft-info is still at the dump of 7 September 20:42 UTC with 731 application roles and 815 delegated scopes, 972 in union, which with the 58 resource-specific rows gives 1,030 Microsoft Graph names, the same figure as yesterday. Azure Storage adds one delegated scope. complete is false because the inventory carries names from other surfaces and from the service that Microsoft's Graph reference does not publish.

Delegated scopes moved from 811 to 815 and the union from 968 to 972. The four new names are all Customer Lockbox scopes and all four are absent from the published permission reference. apis.socNote: The Azure control plane. One delegated scope, user_impersonation, carries an application into Azure Resource Manager with the signed-in user's full Azure RBAC. A grant here is invisible in every Microsoft Graph permission report.
apis.note: Microsoft publishes no permission table for this resource application. The single delegated scope and its GUID are printed in Microsoft's Entra PowerShell reference; nothing else is asserted. Application permissions: Microsoft names none, and none is invented here.
apis.deltaNote: Recounted today from the same source; no change.

apis.name: SharePoint
apis.socNote: The SharePoint resource application is a separate consent surface from Microsoft Graph. Sites.FullControl.All granted here reaches every site collection and every OneDrive in the tenant and does not appear in a Graph permission report. Legacy Azure ACS app-only grants sit outside Entra consent reporting entirely.
apis.note: Microsoft publishes no consolidated permission table for this resource application. The four strings recorded are the ones Microsoft names verbatim for the SharePoint API on the pages read on 29 Aug 2026 — the app-only registration guidance, the Azure AI Search SharePoint ACL page and the Power Platform SharePoint app configuration page. This is a floor, not a complete list, and complete stays false. Baseline run: no previous count to compare against, and that is correct exactly once.
apis.deltaNote: Recounted today from the same source; no change.

apis.name: Microsoft Intune
apis.socNote: Baseline read. Microsoft publishes no consolidated permission list for the Microsoft Intune resource application; it names get_data_warehouse by string in the Data Warehouse app-only authentication guide and nothing else. One permission is recorded because one is what Microsoft prints. The surface stays open rather than being padded with plausible names.
apis.deltaNote: Recounted today from the same source; no change.

apis.name: Microsoft Purview
apis.description: Microsoft Purview data-plane REST APIs — catalog, scanning, account, metadata policy and DevOps policy planes, reached with a token for https://purview.azure.net.
apis.socNote: Read on 1 Sep 2026, on its due date. The Microsoft Purview data plane takes a token for the resource https://purview.azure.net and Microsoft documents NO named delegated or application permission for it: authorisation is decided entirely by Purview's own data-plane roles — Data Curator, Data Source Administrator, Collection Admin, Policy Author. For a SOC this is the finding, not an empty result: an app-consent review of this surface will show nothing, because the grant that matters is a Purview role assignment and it never appears in Entra consent reporting. Zero is a read, not a gap.
apis.deltaNote: Recounted today from the same source; no change.

apis.name: Power BI Service
apis.socNote: Power BI holds tenant-wide reporting data and its admin scopes read every workspace. A grant here does not appear in any Graph permission report.
apis.note: Microsoft publishes no consolidated permission list for the Power BI Service application. The REST API landing page tells the reader to read the list out of the Azure portal's Request API permissions blade instead, and the page the earlier runs pointed at, /power-bi/developer/embedded/power-bi-permissions, now redirects to a generic identity-platform article that names no Power BI scope at all. Each name below was read verbatim from the Required Scope section of one operation page, cited on the entry. apis.name: Azure Storage
apis.socNote: A single delegation scope, user_impersonation, that lets an application do anything the signed-in user can do against Blob, File, Queue and Table. It carries no scoping of its own: what it can reach is decided entirely by the user's Azure RBAC on the storage account, so a consent grant here inherits the blast radius of whoever signs in. Invisible in any Graph permission report.

roles.name: External Identity Provider Administrator
roles.description: Can configure identity providers for use in direct federation.
roles.intro: This is a privileged role. This administrator manages federation between Microsoft Entra organizations and external identity providers. With this role, users can add new identity providers and configure all available settings (e.g. authentication path, service ID, assigned key containers). This user can enable the Microsoft Entra organization to trust authentications from external identity providers. The resulting impact on end-user experiences depends on the type of organization:
tasks: Microsoft Entra organizations for employees and partners: The addition of a federation (e.g. with Gmail) will immediately impact all guest invitations not yet redeemed. See Adding Google as an identity provider for B2B guest users.

Azure Active Directory B2C organizations: The addition of a federation (for example, with Facebook, or with another Microsoft Entra organization) does not immediately impact end-user flows until the identity provider is added as an option in a user flow (also called a built-in policy). See Configuring a Microsoft account as an identity provider for an example. To change user flows, the limited role of "B2C User Flow Administrator" is required.

roles.name: Global Administrator
roles.dateNote: Not dated by Microsoft. This is a correction made in this brief, not an event at Microsoft.
roles.description: Can manage all aspects of Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft services that use Microsoft Entra identities.
roles.impact: Nothing about the role's authority changed. What changed is this page: the privileged-only filter in the Directory actions panel no longer counts the Privileged Identity Management read (or, for Privileged Role Administrator, the PIM allTasks) row, because Microsoft does not label it privileged.
roles.action: If a report or a privileged-action inventory was built from this catalog before 29 August 2026, re-run it: the privileged action row count for these six roles was one too high in each.
roles.intro: This is a privileged role. Users with this role have access to all administrative features in Microsoft Entra ID, as well as services that use Microsoft Entra identities like the Microsoft Defender portal, the Microsoft Purview portal, Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Skype for Business Online. Global Administrators can view Directory Activity logs. Furthermore, Global Administrators can elevate their access to manage all Azure subscriptions and management groups. This allows Global Administrators to get full access to all Azure resources using the respective Microsoft Entra tenant. The person who signs up for the Microsoft Entra organization becomes a Global Administrator. There can be more than one Global Administrator at your company. Global Administrators can reset the password for any user and all other administrators. A Global Administrator cannot remove their own Global Administrator assignment. This is to prevent a situation where an organization has zero Global Administrators.

Global Reader is the read-only counterpart to Global Administrator. Assign Global Reader instead of Global Administrator for planning, audits, or investigations. Use Global Reader in combination with other limited admin roles like Exchange Administrator to make it easier to get work done without the assigning the Global Administrator role. Global Reader works with Microsoft 365 admin center, Exchange admin center, SharePoint admin center, Teams admin center, Microsoft Defender portal, Microsoft Purview portal, Azure portal, and Device Management admin center.

roles.impact: A role widely handed out for reading and configuring security policy becomes able to disable an account, terminate its live sessions and force a credential reset. Nobody consents to it and no assignment changes; the capability simply arrives. It is the same capability Microsoft carved into the deliberately narrow SOC Identity Responder role in June 2026.
roles.action: Pull the current holders and treat the list as a new privileged role. graph.name: SecurityAlert.Create.All
graph.before: did not exist — only SecurityAlert.Read.All and SecurityAlert.ReadWrite.All existed, and neither could create an alert
graph.after: least privileged permission for POST /security/alerts_v2/createAlert. DisplayText "Create security alerts"
graph.impact: An app holding this can inject arbitrary alerts into Defender XDR — title, severity, category, MITRE technique, inline device/user/IP entities, linkToIncident to attach fabricated evidence to a live incident, and isExcludedFromCorrelation to keep it out of correlation.
graph.action: Alert on any consent grant or appRoleAssignment for AppRoleId 06870c4c-7370-4a2a-ad10-239a337af816. Treat alerts with detectionSource: manual or a manual_ providerAlertId prefix as attributable to an API caller rather than a detection.

graph.name: POST /beta/security/alerts_v2/createAlert
graph.before: did not exist — Defender XDR alerts could only be read and updated via Graph
graph.after: bound action on the alerts_v2 collection returning 201 Created, accepting a createAlertInput carrying alert metadata, incident-linking options, workspace routing and inline entity definitions in one request
graph.impact: The alert table is now writable by any consented app, so alert volume and incident content are no longer trustworthy as purely detection-generated.
graph.action: Baseline current alert-creation volume by detectionSource and build a hunting query for alerts whose providerAlertId starts with manual_.

graph.before: beta only — the recovery resource existed at /beta, last published 23 Mar 2026

Recovery operations generate no change notifications and no delta records, so change-tracking detections are blind to them.

graph.name: /v1.0/policies/crossTenantAccessPolicy/{default|partners}/m365Capabilities
graph.consent: Admin consent; delegated non-owner also needs Global Administrator
graph.before: did not exist — Microsoft 365 cross-tenant authorization was governed by the legacy OrgRel model, not by Graph
graph.after: GET, POST and PATCH on the default policy; GET, POST, PATCH and DELETE on partner policies. Partner policy overrides default; the control is inbound-only
graph.impact: A new, GA, externally-facing authorization surface governing which partner tenants can read your users' calendars, MailTips and room bookings — separate from the Entra cross-tenant access policy your CA baseline probably already covers, and API-only for now.
graph.action: Enumerate /policies/crossTenantAccessPolicy/partners and its m365Capabilities now to establish a baseline before this reaches the admin centre UI.

graph.name: Application.ReadWrite.OwnedBy → authenticationBehaviors.coopEnforcement
graph.before: authenticationBehaviors had no Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy control; COOP enforcement was service-controlled and not app-settable
graph.after: new Boolean coopEnforcement — true to enable, false to temporarily suppress, null for the service default — writable through PATCH /applications/{id}
graph.impact: An app that already holds Application.ReadWrite.OwnedBy — commonly granted to CI/CD and app-provisioning tooling — can set coopEnforcement: false and disable a browser-side isolation defence for that app's authentication popups, with no new consent grant and no new permission to trip a consent-monitoring alert.
graph.action: Query /beta/applications?$select=id,appId,authenticationBehaviors and flag any registration with coopEnforcement: false. Treat it as a temporary remediation state that must have an owner and an expiry.

graph.name: Files.ReadWrite.All → assignSensitivityLabel(appliedByUser)
graph.before: an app-only caller applying a sensitivity label was recorded as the application; there was no way to nominate a different acting identity
graph.after: new appliedByUser parameter — Microsoft's wording: "allows app-only callers to specify the user identity on whose behalf the sensitivity label is applied"
graph.impact: The acting identity on a sensitivity-label change is now caller-supplied, so a label downgrade performed by a compromised app-only principal can be attributed in audit to an arbitrary innocent user. Label-change audit records no longer prove which human acted.
graph.action: When investigating sensitivity-label downgrades, correlate the recorded user against the authenticating service principal in the same audit event rather than trusting the user field alone.

graph.name: /beta/security/caseManagement/cases/*/attachments/*/content
graph.before: case evidence content could not be transferred over Graph, and relations and tasks could not be read individually or deleted
graph.after: chunked upload and post-malware-scan download of attachment content, plus GET and DELETE on relations and DELETE on tasks
graph.impact: An app with CaseManagement.ReadWrite.All can exfiltrate raw investigation evidence and destroy the links and tasks that record an investigation's structure — evidence theft and anti-forensics against your own case management, from a single permission.
graph.action: Restrict CaseManagement.ReadWrite.All to named SOAR service principals and alert on DELETE against case relations and tasks.

graph.after: create and manage connections to SAP IAG, carrying the SAP endpoint, OAuth token endpoint, client ID, and the Azure subscription, resource group, key vault and secret name holding its client secret

graph.name: accessReviewReviewerScope → reviewerId, scopeType
graph.consent: Not stated by Microsoft — permissions on the access review APIs are unchanged
graph.before: a reviewer could only be designated through a query expression; principal and resource scoping likewise required a query
graph.after: reviewerId names a reviewer directly by ID, and scopeType selects a well-known scope via new enumerations
graph.impact: Designating the reviewer of a privileged access review is now a single ID field rather than a query an auditor would have to parse, which makes it materially easier for a principal with access-review write rights to install itself or a chosen account as reviewer and rubber-stamp continued privileged access.
graph.action: Re-read reviewerId on your Global Administrator and privileged-role access review definitions and confirm the reviewer is who you expect.

graph.name: User.ReadBasic.All
graph.consent: Application: admin consent required · Delegated: not required
graph.before: returns a basic set of profile properties and, per Microsoft, also app role assignments and license details — behaviour Microsoft describes as accidental
graph.after: returns the basic profile properties only. App role assignments move to User.Read.All and license details to LicenseAssignment.Read.All
graph.impact: Two effects at once. Applications that quietly relied on the extra data break with no deprecation window — Microsoft states no sunset date. And a low-consent scope (delegated User.ReadBasic.All needs no admin consent) stops exposing licence and app-assignment data, which is reconnaissance material for anyone mapping who holds which application role.
graph.action: List service principals granted User.ReadBasic.All and check which of them read app role assignments or licence data. Applications that legitimately need it must be re-consented to User.Read.All or LicenseAssignment.Read.All, both of which require admin consent — so this is a consent-review task, not a code change.

graph.kind: New in service, not yet documented

displayText.Application: Delete all users' authentication methods

descriptionByType.Application: Allows the app to delete authentication methods of all users in your organization, without a signed-in user. Authentication methods include things like a user's phone numbers and Authenticator app settings. This does not allow the app to read, create, or modify authentication methods.

graph.originNote: Live and grantable in the Microsoft Graph service principal, read from Merill's daily service-principal dump on 31 Aug 2026, and absent from Microsoft's published permissions reference on the same date. Microsoft has shipped the permission and has not finished documenting it. Nothing about this is new today at Microsoft — what is new is that this catalog now carries it.
graph.before: not carried by this catalog and not present on Microsoft's permissions reference
graph.after: grantable application permission that deletes other people's authentication methods. Display text: “Delete all users' authentication methods”.
graph.impact: An application holding this can delete a user's registered authentication methods without a signed-in user. Stripping a passkey, a TAP, a hardware OATH token or Windows Hello leaves the account on whatever weaker method survives — the classic pre-step to an MFA-downgrade takeover. It grants no read and no write, so it will not appear in a review that looks for ReadWrite on authentication methods.
graph.action: Query appRoleAssignedTo for each of these thirteen appRoleIds across every service principal in the tenant and alert on any grant. Nothing legitimate outside a purpose-built joiner-mover-leaver tool should hold one. Add the GUIDs to the consent-monitoring watchlist now rather than waiting for the reference page to catch up.

history.note: Entered the catalog. Present in the Graph service principal, absent from Microsoft's permissions reference.

graph.name: GET /v1.0/security/alerts (legacy security alerts API)
graph.dateNote: Microsoft prints the retirement date 15 October 2026 explicitly; the announcement itself is dated only to August 2026.
graph.before: retirement previously scheduled earlier
graph.after: retirement date extended to 15 October 2026
graph.impact: Every SOAR playbook, SIEM connector and script still calling the legacy alerts API stops returning data at retirement. Alert-driven automation fails silently rather than erroring loudly, which is the worse failure mode.
graph.action: Inventory callers of /security/alerts now and move them to /security/alerts_v2 well before 15 October 2026. The date has already moved once, so plan against 15 October and do not assume a third extension.

graph.name: Group.Read.All → onPremisesExtensionAttributes

descriptionByType.Reach: Microsoft added the onPremisesExtensionAttributes property to the group resource on v1.0. extensionAttribute1 through extensionAttribute15, synchronised from on-premises Active Directory, are now readable on groups.

graph.socNote: No consent prompt fires. Every application already holding Group.Read.All or Group.ReadWrite.All starts seeing on-premises extension attributes on groups it could already read. Those attributes routinely carry cost centre, business unit and classification values, and organisations use them as dynamic membership rule inputs. Re-read what your group-reading applications are entitled to see.

graph.name: AgentIdentityBlueprint.ReadWrite.All → isDisabled

descriptionByType.Reach: Microsoft added the isDisabled property to agentIdentityBlueprint on beta, so an agent identity blueprint can be deactivated without being deleted.

graph.socNote: A kill switch for an agent identity that leaves the object in place. Worth wiring into the agent offboarding runbook now, while the surface is still small: disabling beats deleting when an agent has to be stopped during an investigation and its history has to survive.

graph.name: getStatisticsByPolicy method on Microsoft 365 Backup Storage (beta)

descriptionByType.Endpoint: Microsoft added the getStatisticsByPolicy method for Microsoft 365 Backup Storage, returning protection statistics per policy. Microsoft's what's-new entry names the method but does not print the request path, so no path is asserted here.

graph.consent: Admin or user consent, depending on tenant consent policy

descriptionByType.delegated: Allows the application to access Azure Storage on behalf of the signed-in user, taking any action the user is permitted to take by Azure RBAC on the storage account.

adminConsent.delegated: Depends on the tenant user-consent policy

graph.idsNote: Microsoft does not print an appRoleId or oauth2PermissionScope GUID for this scope on the authorization reference, and this brief does not type GUIDs by hand, so the field is omitted.
graph.impact: A grant on this scope is invisible in every Microsoft Graph permission report, because it belongs to a different resource application. Its reach is whatever Azure RBAC gives the signed-in user on the storage account, so on an account holding Storage Blob Data Contributor it is a full read and write of that data.
graph.action: Enumerate delegated grants against the Azure Storage resource application in your tenant and check them against the RBAC held by the users behind them. Treat a grant on an account with data-plane RBAC as a data-access grant, not an infrastructure one.
